messages.subject: Re: Mixed species clusters
messages.body_plain:
> > I am currently using DISTANCE to analyse line transects of herbivores on savannah plains. My problem is that many species occur in mixed clusters. For example, a cluster may consist of 50 individuals of species A and 2 of species B. If I am calculating abundance of species B I have a problem determining the cluster size - the effective cluster size is 52, the actual number of animals is 2. If I use 2 then analysis of the cluster size/distance relationship will be wrong as small clusters would occasionally be visible at large distances because they are part of large, mixed clusters, but if I use 52 the actual number of animals is wrong. Does anyone know of a way of seperating effective and actual cluster sizes?

Probably the best solution is to do a combined analysis.  So for a given
species, extract all clusters for which that species was
represented.  Analyse the data using the full cluster sizes (52 in your
example).  That will give you a correct estimate of cluster density but an
invalid estimate of mean cluster size.  You can use the estimated
detection function to estimate the probability of detection for each of
the detected clusters.  Take a weighted average of the number of animals
of the species of interest in each of these clusters, where the weights
are equal to 1/(estimated prob of detection).  This gives you an estimate
of the mean cluster size for the species of interest, which you can now
use to multiply the estimated cluster density by.  (If this step isn't
obvious, you'll find the formulae in the distance sampling book.)

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Re: Mixed species clusters
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tom, distance list,

Tom Maddox wrote:
> >I am currently using DISTANCE to analyse line transects of
> >herbivores on savannah
> >plains. My problem is that many species occur in mixed clusters.
> >For example,
> >a cluster may consist of 50 individuals of species A and 2 of species B.
[...]

Steve Buckland replied:
> >Probably the best solution is to do a combined analysis.
[...]

Ken Burnham wrote to suggest an alternative to the combined analysis that
Steve described.  To do it, you'd need to use the new multiple covariates
analysis engine (MCDS) in Distance 4.  In the observation layer, you would
have one column for species, one for cluster size for that species, and one
for combined cluster size for the group.  So, for example, if cluster size is
50 for species A and 2 for species B, recorded at 33.2 meters, you'd have two
records:

Species  Cluster_size  Combined_cluster    Perp distance
A          50             52                   33.2
B           2             52                   33.2

You'd use a data filter to select out only one species.  For this species,
you use Combined_cluster as a covariate in the Detection Function |
Covariates tab of the model definition.  This gives you estimated detection
function, allowing for cluster size.

To calculate abundance for each species, you'd then use the approach outlined
by Steve:

abundance = sum over clusters of (          cluster_size            )
                                 (----------------------------------)
                                 (estimated probability of detection)

This is sometimes called a "Horvitz-Thompson-like estimate".

I read Ken's email, and thought the method could be extended further in two
ways:

- when detection probabilities for the two species are very heterogeneous, we
may be able to do better than using Combined_cluster as the covariate.  We
could try 3 covariates: cluster size of species A, cluster size of species B,
and Combined_cluster; and see which (or which combination) gives the best
model fit.

Species  Cs_A  Cs_b   Combined_cluster    Perp distance
A          50     2         52                   33.2
B           2    50         52                   33.2

Use a data filter to select out only one species.  Then try, for example,
Cs_A and Combined_cluster as covariables.  Of course, they are correlated.
It's best to use some biological intuition if possible -- e.g., if species A
is bright and showy and species B is dull and quiet then cluster size of
species A alone is likely to work better than B or A+B.

- for going from density of clusters to density of individuals, the Horvitz-
Thompson-like method should work fine, so long as estiamted probability of
detection is not too low.  (If estimated probability of detection gets low,
you get unreliable results, as you're calculating 1/probability.)  However,
you can't do this calculation directly in Distance 4.0.  Instead, you have to
read the parameter estimates from the Results tab, then calculate probability
of detection by hand for each cluster, and then do the cluster
size/probability calculation by hand.  Also, variance estimation in this
approach is usually done using bootstrapping -- not practical without some
software!

An alternative is to use the size-bias methods already available in Distance
- e.g., regression of ln(cluster size) on perpendicular distance.  (I think
using ln(cluster size) might work better than ln(g(x)) in this case.)  This
approach makes more assumptions than the non-parametric Horvitz-Thompson-like
method, but can be done in D4 and allows variance estimation.

If you're going to pursue these, I'd advise waiting for the next beta of
Distance 4.0 to come out (very shortly, hopefully), as the MCDS engine will
work much better in the new release.

Hope this all makes some kind of sense!

Cheers,

 - Len Thomas

--
Len Thomas (l...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk)
Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
Mathematical Institute, University of St Andrews
Scotland

messages.body_plain:
Apologies - I should have clarified the following:

> >- for going from density of clusters to density of individuals, the Horvitz-
> >Thompson-like method should work fine, so long as estiamted probability of
> >detection is not too low.  (If estimated probability of detection gets low,
> >you get unreliable results, as you're calculating 1/probability.)  However,
> >you can't do this calculation directly in Distance 4.0.

[...]

You can't do the calculation directly in Distance 4.0 if you're only using the
the Combined_cluster field as covariate.  If you're using the actual cluster
size for the species as an additional (or alternative) covariate (e.g., for
species A, the Cs_A field) then you can indeed do the Horvitz-Thompson-like
method in Distance 4.  Simply click on the "cluster size" box beside the
appropriate covariate, in the Detection Function | Covariates tab of the Model
Definition.  Distance will do the rest.  If you want variance estimates, you
need to bootstrap.

Sorry again for the previous omission.

 - Len

messages.subject: modelling observer bias at point counts
messages.subject_clean: modelling observer bias at point counts
messages.body_plain:
Dear mailing list,

I am working on a project that involves a distance sampling spotlight
survey of mammals around the south-west of the UK, using variable
circular plots.  We have carried out several thousand point counts in
varying conditions, with different observers.  I am interested in
investigating the effects of these factors i.e. observer, weather, time
of night etc. on the frequency of observations of the different
species.  The frequency data for all species have poisson distributions,
with a large number of zeros (i.e. no observations at a point count).  I
was thinking of using a generalised linear model (GLM), with individual
point counts as the sampling unit. However, we are quantifying the
effort at each point by taking the proportion of 360 degrees that has an
unobstructed view over the surrounding habitat.  I'm not sure how to
analyse the data once it is standardised for effort at each point.  Can
I still carry out a GLM in some shape or form?  Any suggestions would be
gratefully received.

Many thanks,

John Davison
j.da...@csl.gov.uk

messages.subject: Re: Using post stratification for non equal repeat surveys
messages.subject_clean: Using post stratification for non equal repeat surveys
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tom, list,

The behaviour you describe for Distance 3.5 is "by design" - although I admit
that it is not clearly set out in the manual. When you stratify by a field in
the observation layer, Distance reproduces all of the samples in each of the
new "post-strata", regardless of whether they contain observations or not.
Generally this is the right thing to do. For example, imagine you recorded
the sex of the animals you observed, and you want to try an analysis post-
stratified by sex. Imagine you have 30 transects, but on 10 of them you only
saw female animals. If Distance didn't reproduce all of the samples in the
"female" post-stratum, then density in that stratum would be based on a
sample of only the 20 transects with observations -- and so would be over-
estimated.

In the case you describe, leaving out samples with no observations isn't the
right thing to do either. Imagine the case where you saw no animals on one
transect in one month. That transect would be left out of the post-stratum
for that month -- again resulting in an over-estimate of density.

How can you get around this problem? The answer is to use Distance 4.0. D4
allows for more than one sample layer, which is exactly what you want. You'd
define a Sample layer for transect, and a SubSample1 layer for Month. Then,
in the Model Definition properties, you would post-stratify by the SubSample1
layer.  If you want the correct density estimates, you need to have the
length of each transect in the Month layer (i.e. length is repeated for each
month), and you need to specify this field as the effort field in the Survey
Properties | Data Fields page.

The only problem in this solution is the variances.  Ideally, you'd like to
be able to treat the transects as the samples - for example if you bootstrap
you want to resample transects across months.  Unfortunately, you can't do
this in Distance, so you'll have to be content with resampling transects
within months (ie samples within (post-)strata) - this ignores the connection
between, say, transect 1 in month 1 and transect 1 in month 2.

While answering this query, I discovered a bug in the post-stratification
option of Distance 4, so if you want to use the above suggestion, I'd wait
for the next beta! - due out in the next few days.  (New beta versions are
announced on the distance-4-beta list - see archives of this list for how to
join.)

Hope this helps.

 - Len Thomas

--

Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
Mathematical Institute, University of St Andrews
Scotland KY16 9SS
